clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic PLA2G6 variants, part of the PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration (PLAN) spectrum and a subtype of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation.
Classic onset is in late infancy with psychomotor regression, truncal hypotonia and progressive loss of previously acquired motor and cognitive milestones.
Hypotonia often evolves into spasticity and pyramidal signs, producing a mixed picture of central and peripheral involvement over time.
Visual impairment with optic atrophy and, frequently, an abnormal or extinguished electroretinogram is characteristic, and strabismus/nystagmus are common.
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography may reveal denervation, and characteristic axonal spheroids are the pathological hallmark.
MRI typically shows cerebellar atrophy, often with T2 signal change, and iron deposition in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra tends to appear later in the disease.
A clue on MRI is the presence of claval hypertrophy and cerebellar atrophy; iron accumulation may be absent early, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary — seizure control, spasticity management, feeding and respiratory support — as no disease-modifying therapy currently exists.
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy results from loss-of-function variants in PLA2G6, which encodes a calcium-independent phospholipase A2 (iPLA2-VIA) that hydrolyses glycerophospholipids at the sn-2 position and is central to membrane phospholipid remodelling, fatty-acid release and maintenance of membrane homeostasis. Deficient enzyme activity disturbs the balance of membrane lipids and promotes accumulation of oxidised and abnormal phospholipids, impairing mitochondrial and membrane integrity in neurons and their axons. This leads to widespread axonal degeneration with formation of characteristic dystrophic axonal 'spheroids' — swellings packed with disorganised tubulovesicular and membranous material — throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems, hence the neuroaxonal designation. Cerebellar Purkinje and granule cell loss produces the early and severe cerebellar atrophy seen on imaging, while progressive dysfunction of the retina and optic pathways causes optic atrophy and electroretinographic abnormalities. Impaired lipid handling secondarily drives iron accumulation in the basal ganglia, particularly the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, linking the disorder to the neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation spectrum, though this iron deposition characteristically develops later than the clinical and cerebellar changes.
additionalDifferentials: Other neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation subtypes (e.g. PKAN/pantothenate kinase-associated)
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses and other neuronal storage disorders
Ataxia-telangiectasia and other early-onset progressive ataxias
Spinal muscular atrophy or other causes of infantile hypotonia with regression
additionalInvestigations: PLA2G6 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, or a NBIA/neurodegeneration gene panel
Brain MRI including iron-sensitive sequences for cerebellar atrophy and pallidal/nigral iron
Electroretinography and ophthalmological assessment for retinal and optic nerve involvement
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography for associated neuropathy/denervation
Electroencephalography for epileptiform activity and characteristic fast rhythms
Visual evoked potentials to assess optic pathway function
redFlags: Loss of previously acquired developmental milestones (regression)
Rapidly progressive visual failure with optic atrophy
Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration or respiratory compromise
Progressive spasticity and loss of ambulation in a young child
reference.prognosis: The classic infantile form is relentlessly progressive, with loss of motor and cognitive function, and survival is typically limited to childhood, often with death from respiratory complications. Later-onset atypical PLAN variants may progress more slowly, but no disease-modifying treatment is currently available.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because brain iron accumulation is not yet visible, since iron deposition often appears late
Missing the diagnosis in a hypotonic infant by not recognising early cerebellar atrophy on MRI
Overlooking retinal involvement by not performing electroretinography
Attributing the picture to a primary neuromuscular disorder when there is prominent central and axonal pathology
Failing to arrange genetic counselling and carrier testing for an autosomal recessive condition
references: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation review literature (source-neutral)
